newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel lowers interest rates 0.5 point.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel lowers interest rates 0.5 point.

text.p: The Bank of Israel said on Monday it would lower its key lending rate for February, but analysts and traders said the 0.5 percentage point cut was cautious and would do little to ease pressure on the shekel exchange rate.
The cut, which takes effect on Thursday, brings the base lending rate to 14.2 percent. The rate is the one charged commercial banks at daily and weekly monetary tenders.

The central bank said it had cut rates 2.8 percentage points since August from a peak of 17 percent. But inflation has fallen from a 14.6 percent annualised rate in the first-half of 1996 to less than half that in the second, according to Bank Hapoalim estimates.

"It was (the reduction) expected, no surprises. They put a lot of pressure on (Bank of Israel Governor Jacob) Frenkel to lower more but he was very cautious. It won't influence shares or the forex market," said Tzvi Hoffman of Meitav Securities and Investments.

Analysts said the bank faces pressure to keep lowering rates to prevent the shekel from strengthening too much against the basket of currencies to which it is officially linked. The bank sees the currency band as a key facet in achieving monetary stability.

The shekel on Monday fell to an all-time low against the dollar. However, the weakness of other currencies in the basket has caused the basket rate to fall over the last two weeks to the bottom end of its official trading band.
The Bank of Israel has been forced to intervene heavily in the local foreign exchange market, injecting what currency traders estimated was about $500 million into the economy.
Jonathan Katz, chief economist at Solid Financial Markets, said the lower inflationary trend and a slowing economy were also encouraging the bank to ease rates.
The slowing trend has recently grown worse, with the Bank of Israel's "S" index of economic performance falling one percent over November and December.
Katz is now forecasting that the economy will grow three percent this year, down from the 3.7 percent he had earlier forecast.

However, the central bank must also contend with the budget deficit, which analysts said was making it cautious. Although the official budget aims to keep the deficit to 2.8 percent of gross domestic product, analysts said January spending was probably running ahead of projections.
